concepts.name: Economic choices, needs and wants, and scarcity
concepts.description: Choices made by individuals, enterprises and governments, the difference between needs and wants, unlimited wants and scarce resources.
concepts.idea: Every economic choice arises because wants are unlimited but resources are limited.
concepts.rule: Needs are essentials such as food, water and shelter; wants are things like gadgets, vacations and luxuries. Human wants are unlimited and keep changing. Resources (land, labour, capital, technology) are limited and have alternative uses, so they are scarce.
concepts.example: Steel can be used for buildings, vehicles or tools, so choosing one use means giving up others.

questions.q: Which of the following is a need?
questions.a: food

questions.q: Human wants are
questions.a: unlimited and keep changing

questions.q: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and ____.
questions.a: technology

questions.q: Who makes economic choices?
questions.a: individuals, enterprises and governments

questions.q: A want is
questions.a: something we desire such as gadgets, vacations or luxury items
o: something we desire such as gadgets, vacations or luxury items

questions.q: Resources are scarce because
questions.a: they are limited in quantity but have many alternative uses
o: they are limited in quantity but have many alternative uses

questions.q: When wants exceed resources, people and governments must
questions.a: choose how to use resources

questions.q: Which is an example of an economic choice by a government?
questions.a: spending on highways or hospitals

questions.q: Explain the difference between needs and wants with two examples of each.
questions.a: Needs are essentials such as food, water and shelter. Wants are things we desire but can live without, such as gadgets, vacations and luxury items.

questions.q: A farmer choosing between growing wheat or barley on limited land is making
questions.a: an economic choice

questions.q: Natural and human resources are limited in ____.
questions.a: quantity

questions.q: Five library copies for twenty students show
questions.a: scarcity of resources relative to wants
o: scarcity of resources relative to wants

questions.q: Classify as need or want: rice, a smartphone upgrade, drinking water, a vacation.
questions.a: Rice and drinking water are needs; a smartphone upgrade and a vacation are wants.

questions.q: Why can a country not satisfy all wants of its people?
questions.a: Wants are unlimited and keep changing, while resources such as land, labour, capital and technology are limited, so not all wants can be met.

questions.q: Give three examples of economic choices made by an individual, an enterprise and a government.
questions.a: Individual: spending pocket money on snacks or saving for shoes. Enterprise: employing more labour or more capital in production. Government: spending on highways or hospitals.

questions.q: Why do wants create pressure on resources?
questions.a: Because unlimited wants keep growing while resources remain limited
o: Because unlimited wants keep growing while resources remain limited

questions.q: How do wants change over time? Give an example from the chapter.
questions.a: Wants keep changing; a person may want to upgrade from a bicycle to a motorbike and then to a car.
s: Bicycle to motorbike or similar example

questions.q: Explain why scarcity forces individuals, enterprises and governments to make choices.
questions.a: Resources have alternative uses and are limited, but wants are unlimited. So each must decide how to use resources in the best possible way, choosing some uses and giving up others.
s: Need to choose and give up options

questions.q: Ravi says everything we buy is a need. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Needs are essentials like food, water and shelter, while many things we buy, such as gadgets, vacations and luxury items, are wants.
s: Distinguishes needs and wants with examples

questions.q: List three things your family bought this month and classify each as a need or a want with a reason.
questions.a: Vegetables: need, essential food. Medicines: need, for health. A new video game: want, not essential.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost and the production possibility curve
concepts.description: Opportunity cost as the value of the option given up, and the production possibility curve as a picture of trade-offs.
concepts.idea: Choosing one alternative means giving up others, and the value of what is given up is the opportunity cost.
concepts.rule: Opportunity cost is the value of what is given up when a choice is made. The Production Possibility Curve (PPC) shows combinations of two goods (for example barley and wheat) that can be produced with efficient use of resources; it slopes downward because more of one means less of the other.
concepts.example: A farmer who grows more barley must give up some wheat; that wheat is the opportunity cost of the barley.

questions.q: The value of what is given up when one alternative is chosen is called
questions.a: opportunity cost

questions.q: The Production Possibility Curve shows
questions.a: the trade-off between two goods that can be produced
o: the trade-off between two goods that can be produced

questions.q: On the PPC of barley and wheat, the curve slopes ____.
questions.a: downward

questions.q: All points on the PPC show
questions.a: the maximum output through efficient use of resources
o: the maximum output through efficient use of resources

questions.q: If a farmer grows more barley, the wheat produced
questions.a: decreases because resources are limited

questions.q: The opportunity cost of growing more barley is
questions.a: the wheat given up

questions.q: A PPC helps enterprises and governments by
questions.a: supporting better planning and decision-making

questions.q: On a PPC, moving from point A to point E means producing
questions.a: more barley and less wheat

questions.q: Explain why the PPC slopes downward.
questions.a: With limited land, water and labour, producing more of one crop requires shifting resources away from the other, so the output of the second falls.
s: More of one means less of the other

questions.q: A student has Rs 100 and must choose between a notebook and saving for a tennis racket. The economic concept is
questions.a: opportunity cost

questions.q: If you spend Rs 100 on snacks and give up buying a book, the book is the ____ cost.
questions.a: opportunity

questions.q: A farmer chooses to grow wheat on all the land. The opportunity cost is
questions.a: the barley that could have been grown
o: the barley that could have been grown

questions.q: What is your opportunity cost when you spend an hour watching TV instead of studying?
questions.a: The value of what the hour could have been used for, such as studying or revision, which is given up.
s: Identifies time as a scarce resource

questions.q: A PPC plots barley on the x-axis and wheat on the y-axis. What do the points on it show?
questions.a: Each point shows a combination of barley and wheat that can be produced using all resources efficiently without waste.

questions.q: A farmer can grow barley or wheat on limited land. Explain the trade-off and opportunity cost.
questions.a: Since land, water and labour are limited, growing more barley means some wheat must be sacrificed. The wheat given up is the opportunity cost of the extra barley. The PPC shows this trade-off along a downward slope.
s: Wheat sacrificed as the opportunity cost
PPC downward slope shows the trade-off

questions.q: Understanding opportunity cost helps a decision-maker to
questions.a: compare alternatives and their consequences

questions.q: Is time a scarce resource? Explain with opportunity cost.
questions.a: Yes. There are only 24 hours in a day; using an hour for one activity means giving up other uses of it, so each choice has an opportunity cost.
s: Choosing one use gives up another

questions.q: Explain how opportunity cost improves the quality of decisions of a family, an enterprise and the government.
questions.a: A family compares what it gives up when buying one item over another; an enterprise weighs alternative production choices and their gains; a government weighs spending on one sector against another. Considering what is given up leads to better use of limited resources.

questions.q: Sam says a choice that costs no money has no opportunity cost. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up, which can be time or effort, not just money.
s: Says cost includes forgone alternatives such as time

questions.q: Create a two-good PPC example for a school canteen making samosas and sandwiches and describe the trade-off.
questions.a: With a fixed number of workers and oven time, making more samosas means fewer sandwiches; the sandwiches given up are the opportunity cost of extra samosas.

concepts.name: What economics is: household management, decisions and data
concepts.description: The meaning and origin of economics, how economic entities interact, the need for data and analysis, and the Economic Survey.
concepts.idea: Economics studies how choices are made by optimising the use of limited resources to satisfy needs and wants, and good decisions rely on data.
concepts.rule: Economics comes from the Greek oikonomia (oikos, household; nemein, management). It deals with consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions. Good decisions rely on data and analysis. The Economic Survey, prepared by the Ministry of Finance, is presented in Parliament before the Union Budget.
concepts.example: Families divide money among essentials, non-essentials and savings; governments plan spending from tax revenue.

questions.q: The word economics comes from the Greek word
questions.a: oikonomia

questions.q: Oikos means
questions.a: household

questions.q: Economics refers to ____ management.
questions.a: household

questions.q: The Economic Survey is prepared by the
questions.a: Ministry of Finance

questions.q: Economics deals with how choices are made by
questions.a: optimising the use of limited resources to satisfy needs and wants
o: optimising the use of limited resources to satisfy needs and wants

questions.q: Which are economic entities that interact in an economy?
questions.a: consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions
o: consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions

questions.q: The Economic Survey is presented in Parliament
questions.a: before the Union Budget

questions.q: Good economic decisions rely on
questions.a: data and analysis, not guesswork

questions.q: Why is economics called household management on a national scale?
questions.a: Like families, nations have limited resources and must plan how to use them efficiently, so not only families but nations manage resources.
s: Families and nations have limited resources

questions.q: Families allocate their money for
questions.a: essential items, non-essential items and savings
o: essential items, non-essential items and savings

questions.q: Governments use revenue from ____ to plan expenditure on infrastructure and welfare.
questions.a: taxation

questions.q: Enterprises study market trends in order to
questions.a: serve customers better and maximise profits
o: serve customers better and maximise profits

questions.q: Give two examples of essential and two of non-essential family spending from the chapter.
questions.a: Essential: food, medicines, school supplies. Non-essential: jewellery, entertainment, restaurant meals.

questions.q: What does the Economic Survey contain?
questions.a: It reviews the economy's performance in the past year and analyses sectors such as agriculture, industry, services, employment, inflation, education, health and infrastructure, and discusses future challenges and opportunities.

questions.q: Explain how economists help individuals, enterprises and institutions take decisions.
questions.a: They study the available alternatives, the opportunity costs and possible outcomes, using data from government reports such as economic surveys and company financial statements. Their analysis helps understand risks and opportunities.

questions.q: Why is the Economic Survey called a blueprint for the Union Budget?
questions.a: It gives policymakers insights for making budget decisions
o: It gives policymakers insights for making budget decisions

questions.q: Can effective economic decisions be made without reliable data? Give an example.
questions.a: No. For example, a government planning how much to spend on schools needs data on enrolment and needs; without it money may be wasted.

questions.q: Explain how an economy involves how people earn, how prices are set and how government policy affects markets.
questions.a: People work and earn wages, wealth and resources are distributed, prices are determined in the market, education and technology drive investment, and government policies and trade influence prices. Economics studies these interactions.

questions.q: Tara says economics is only about money. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Economics is about how choices are made with limited resources, involving consumers, producers, governments and institutions, not only money.

questions.q: Choose a commodity in the news (such as vegetables or fuel) and explain a production decision that producers might make and why.
questions.a: For example, farmers deciding how much tomato to grow depends on last year's prices, rainfall and demand; more supply may lower price, so they weigh how much to produce.
s: Gives factors such as price or demand

concepts.name: The three key questions: what, how and for whom to produce
concepts.description: The central questions every economy must answer, with examples, and labour-intensive and capital-intensive production.
concepts.idea: Because wants exceed resources every economy must decide what, how and for whom to produce.
concepts.rule: What to produce: which goods and in what quantities. How to produce: which methods and technologies, labour-intensive or capital-intensive. For whom to produce: which consumers will be served given income levels, tastes and needs.
concepts.example: Farmers choosing sugarcane and paddy or millets and pulses face a trade-off between short-term gains and long-term sustainability.

questions.q: The three key economic questions are
questions.a: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce
o: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce
when to sleep, eat and work
what to buy, sell and save

questions.q: Production using more workers and less machinery is
questions.a: labour-intensive

questions.q: Production using more machines and fewer workers is called ____-intensive.
questions.a: capital

questions.q: Agriculture and handicrafts usually rely more on
questions.a: labour

questions.q: The question "what to produce" is about
questions.a: which goods and services and in what quantities
o: which goods and services and in what quantities

questions.q: The question "for whom to produce" is about
questions.a: the purpose of goods and who benefits from them
o: the purpose of goods and who benefits from them

questions.q: The question "how to produce" is about
questions.a: the methods, resources and technologies used
o: the methods, resources and technologies used

questions.q: Different types of shoes such as school shoes and sports shoes show
questions.a: producers decide which consumer group to serve
o: producers decide which consumer group to serve

questions.q: Explain the trade-off in choosing between sugarcane and millets and pulses.
questions.a: Sugarcane gives high profits and supports sugar industries but uses much water. Millets and pulses save water, improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. The choice trades short-term gains against long-term sustainability.

questions.q: Steel and automobile manufacturing usually depend more on
questions.a: machinery

questions.q: School shoes are usually simple in design, durable and ____.
questions.a: affordable

questions.q: A garment manufacturer will rely more on labour if
questions.a: machines are expensive and labour is cheap
o: machines are expensive and labour is cheap
machines are cheap and labour is costly

questions.q: Name two factors that decide whether a firm uses labour-intensive or capital-intensive production.
questions.a: The cost of capital, level of technology, nature of the product, availability and relative cost of labour, and government laws.

questions.q: Why are customised designer clothes made with skilled labour while mass-produced garments use machines?
questions.a: Customised clothes need individual skill and care, whereas large quantities of similar garments are produced faster and cheaper by machines.

questions.q: Explain the "for whom to produce" question using footwear as an example.
questions.a: Producers decide which group to serve depending on needs and purchasing power: school shoes for students (simple, durable), office shoes for professionals (formal, leather), sports shoes for athletes (grip, light) and casual shoes for daily use. Materials depend on the target group.

questions.q: Why must producers study consumers before deciding what to make?
questions.a: To ensure limited resources are used to meet real demand
o: To ensure limited resources are used to meet real demand

questions.q: Should the government spend more on healthcare and education or on defence? What economic idea decides this?
questions.a: The government has limited funds, so spending more in one area means less in another. It must weigh the opportunity cost and the needs of the people.

questions.q: Explain how the three key questions are connected for a farmer growing crops.
questions.a: What to produce: choose crops such as paddy or millets. How to produce: use more labour or machines and irrigation methods. For whom to produce: decide whether to sell in the market or for local consumers, depending on demand and income.

questions.q: Ali says producers should always choose the most profitable crop. Evaluate.
questions.a: Not always. The most profitable crop, like sugarcane, may use much water and harm long-term soil health, so producers should also consider sustainability and opportunity costs.
s: States it is not always right
Gives sustainability or opportunity cost reason

questions.q: Suppose you start a small bakery. Answer the three key economic questions for it.
questions.a: What: bread and cakes in given quantities. How: decide between hand kneading (labour) and a mixing machine (capital). For whom: local families and school children with affordable prices.

concepts.name: Economic systems: planned, market and mixed
concepts.description: How different economic systems answer the key questions, and how India moved from a state-led approach to a mixed economy after 1991.
concepts.idea: An economic system decides who controls production, consumption and distribution.
concepts.rule: Planned economy: a central authority decides what, how and for whom; the government owns most resources; examples the former Soviet Union, North Korea, Cuba. Market economy: demand and supply decide; private ownership; government acts as a referee; examples USA, Japan, Hong Kong. Mixed economy: both; examples India (post-1991), China (post-1978), Germany, Sweden.
concepts.example: By 1991 India faced serious economic difficulties, and reforms encouraged private enterprise and opened the economy to global trade and investment.

questions.q: In a planned economy the main decisions are made by
questions.a: a central planning authority of the government
o: a central planning authority of the government

questions.q: In a market economy decisions are mainly made by
questions.a: demand and supply with little government intervention
o: demand and supply with little government intervention

questions.q: An economy that combines features of market and planned economies is called a ____ economy.
questions.a: mixed

questions.q: Which is an example of a planned economy?
questions.a: the former Soviet Union

questions.q: In a planned economy the government owns
questions.a: most resources and sectors such as land, factories, banks and transport
o: most resources and sectors such as land, factories, banks and transport

questions.q: In a market economy the government acts like
questions.a: a referee, ensuring safety and law and order
o: a referee, ensuring safety and law and order

questions.q: Competition among many producers in a market economy encourages
questions.a: better quality, lower prices and innovation
o: better quality, lower prices and innovation

questions.q: A weakness of a planned economy is
questions.a: little motivation for enterprises to improve quality or innovate
o: little motivation for enterprises to improve quality or innovate

questions.q: Why is the government said to act like a referee in a market economy?
questions.a: It ensures safety and law and order and does not control prices or production, just as a referee ensures the rules are followed but does not play.
s: Does not control prices or production

questions.q: India (post-1991) is an example of
questions.a: a mixed economy

questions.q: China after ____ is given as an example of a mixed economy.
After independence India followed
questions.a: a more state-led approach similar to a planned economy
o: a more state-led approach similar to a planned economy

questions.q: Name two features of a market economy from the chapter.
questions.a: Ownership of resources mainly with individuals and private companies; many producers offering similar products; prices decided by demand and supply.

questions.q: Give one example each of a planned, market and mixed economy.
questions.a: Planned: former Soviet Union, North Korea or Cuba. Market: USA, Japan or Hong Kong. Mixed: India (post-1991), China (post-1978), Germany or Sweden.

questions.q: Explain the reforms of 1991 and their effect on India's economic system.
questions.a: By 1991 India faced serious economic difficulties. The government reduced excessive regulations, encouraged private enterprise, opened the economy to global trade and investment and increased competition. This moved India towards a more market-oriented system while keeping an important role for the government.
s: More market-oriented but with government role

questions.q: Why do pure economic systems rarely exist in reality?
questions.a: Most economies combine private ownership with some government regulation
o: Most economies combine private ownership with some government regulation

questions.q: Why is a mixed economy considered practical?
questions.a: It combines the efficiency, competition and innovation of markets with government regulation and welfare, so it addresses limits of both pure systems.
s: Combines strengths of market and planned systems

questions.q: Compare planned and market economies on ownership, decision-making and competition.
questions.a: Planned: government owns most resources, a central authority decides, competition is restricted by licences. Market: private individuals and firms own resources, demand and supply decide, competition among producers is strong.

questions.q: Meera says in a market economy the government has no role. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Even in market economies governments play an important role, ensuring safety, law and order and some regulation, as in the USA and Singapore.

questions.q: Which economic system do you think best promotes innovation and which gives the most freedom? Give reasons.
questions.a: A market or mixed economy promotes innovation because competition rewards new ideas, and it gives freedom of choice to producers and consumers, while government keeps fairness and safety through regulation.
s: Names a system for innovation with a reason
Names a system for freedom with a reason
